text:
this week was an insane launch of @SOTAwives - some thoughts going into the weekend on how to host an epic launch:

1/ lean into haters: we went over getting canceled as part of the pod on purpose, and my haters came out on youtube - thanks for the extra engagement friends ;) 

2/ don't be passive aggressive: so many little decisions to be made, for a good working partnership you have to just agree to disagree. Sarah and I didn't agree on everything (down to the color of the bag charms) and we just had it out over coffee / text / phone and cranked it all out. no tears were shed (this time around at least ❤️)

3/ parties are worth it: the party was probably the most time consuming thing in our whole launch budget but ended up having the most ROI. we showed the pod trailer during the party, and everyone was so supportive quote tweeting / engaging on sunday when the trailer launched + monday when the full ep dropped. also got us incredible photos that people could use for the launch as well 

3/ use your agents: holy crap my codex and muse were going haywire scraping my twitter followers for people who could engage with us + invite to the launch party. back in the day i'd send this to a data entry person in the PH or something so it's crazy to see what you can do now solo 

4/ use your brain: we manually replied to all the QTs / replies and started defining our brand voice. you should see if you can tell who is manning the account at a given time, some millennial vs. gen-z vibes for sure

5/ put yourself out there - people want to support: I know launching another podcast is cliche at this point but we've been floored by how many people actually texted us to say they watched the whole thing and which clips were their favorites - I honestly felt kind of cringe but seeing the response has been so awesome. 

fin/ most important - get yourself a partner in crime 👯🏻‍♀️ @MilksandMatcha is our taskmaster and I am the sidekick. @AnjneyMidha and @tyler_fong_ have also been absolute champs

text:
My thoughts on getting married young as someone who got married at 25 and is still very career driven

1. It is underratedly rewarding to find someone before you are successful. The number of times I have heard “series A then I’ll date” only to lead to “series B then I’ll date” six months later. I made a fraction of what I make now in an extremely IC position when I met Tyler and there is nothing better than knowing we got here together. 

2. Two years ago, my husband went through and acquisition and joined NVIDIA. Half of the team had partners and or was married, the other half was single. We appreciate the fact we met pre-acq because there was never any question of whether someone is with you for the $$. Not that it would be a problem, but why have things spoil the relationship when it doesn’t need to. 

3. Dating takes an absurd amount of time and emotional bandwidth and imagine if you just didn’t have to do that. 

4. You can take a lot more risks with your career and personal life because you have another person to keep you emotionally and financially stable. If you take these big financial bets and they are successful then INCREDIBLE. If they are not successful, you will still be perfectly fine. 

5. You pool your networks together and you know probably 50% more people (assuming you also have heavy overlap) and this is extremely helpful and makes me feel better when I stay at home on a Friday night 😅

6. In many ways the person you marry is an investment and the earlier you invest the better the outcomes! But more seriously, I optimized for a partner who I could grow a lot with in a very complimentary way. And this has worked out nicely.

Multiple interesting stories. Interesting new genre of podcast for tech.

text:
Scientists tracked 5,000 married people for five years to see who got promoted. The thing that predicted it best had nothing on the resume. It was how organized your spouse is. Raises, promotions, even liking your job. Same result for men and women, same result whether both of you worked or only one.

That’s a Washington University study in Psychological Science, and the mechanics are pretty plain once you hear them. A conscientious partner picks up the bills, the groceries, the logistics. You start copying their habits. And a calm house lowers the stress floor that everything else at work sits on top of.

Now look at who nobody asks about this. Jeff Bezos got married in September 1993 and started Amazon ten months later. Jensen Huang married Lori in 1985, eight years before Nvidia existed. Satya Nadella got married and joined Microsoft in the same year, 1992. Not one of them has ever been asked whether the wedding cost them ambition.

Two women who run developer experience at Cerebras and a partnership at Y Combinator get asked it four minutes into their own podcast.

The age data is even less kind to the question. MIT and Kellogg pulled every US founder from 2007 to 2014. Average age at the fastest-growing 0.1% of companies was 45. The 25-year-old in the hoodie gets the magazine cover. The 45-year-old with a mortgage and a spouse gets the exit.

Picking the right person at 25 is the highest-leverage hire most founders ever make, and the only one they can’t fire.

Sarah and Vivian built SOTA Wives around exactly that trade, told by two people who made it. One of them turned down startup funding to finish MIT. Both still ended up at Cerebras and YC. The ambition compounded the whole time.
